A joint resolution approving 'all necessary measures' by the President to repel attacks on U.S. forces and prevent further aggression in Southeast Asia. It became the legal foundation for the escalation of the Vietnam War.

::: {.official-links}
**Read the law** (official GovInfo text)

[Enacted text: 78 Stat. 384](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/statute/78/384){.btn-official}
:::

## Key provisions

- Approved and supported the President's determination to take all necessary measures to repel armed attack and prevent further aggression.
- Authorized force to assist any member or protocol state of the Southeast Asia Collective Defense Treaty that requested help.
- Would expire when the President determined peace was secured, or earlier by concurrent resolution of Congress.

## Why it matters

Its open-ended wording, and later doubts about the incident that prompted it, shaped the congressional backlash that produced the [War Powers Resolution](wpr-1973.qmd) and the wider reassertion statutes of the 1970s.

## Current status

Repealed in January 1971 by section 12 of Pub. L. 91-672, an amendment to the Foreign Military Sales Act.

## Where it sits

- **Layer.** Specific authorization. Laws aimed at a particular conflict, country, program, or problem. Most work through a framework statute: an AUMF through the War Powers Resolution, a sanctions act through IEEPA. ([How the layers work](../study/index.qmd#the-authority-stack))
- **Era.** Vietnam, Watergate, and reassertion ([timeline](../study/timeline.qmd)).
